Nebuchadnezzar II. He ruled Neo-Babylon from 605 to 562 BCE and stands as the greatest king in that dynasty, transforming the city into the ancient world's most magnificent metropolis. A military conqueror who extended Babylonian dominion across the Levant and into Egypt, he rebuilt Babylon with monumental architecture and engineering marvels, most famously the legendary Hanging Gardens. His reign marked the apex of Mesopotamian civilization before Persia's rise. Nebuchadnezzar inherited the throne from his father Nabopolassar, the founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and immediately began expanding Babylonian territory through aggressive military campaigns across the Levant. He conquered Judah and destroyed the Temple of Jerusalem in 586 BCE, exiling the Jewish population to Babylon in captivity, a pivotal event recorded in biblical texts and Babylonian chronicles alike. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon with massive city walls, the celebrated Ishtar Gate decorated with brilliant blue-glazed brick, and reconstructed the legendary Tower of Babel, making it the ancient world's most imposing capital. He commissioned the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, allegedly built for his homesick Median wife Amytis to remind her of her homeland's mountainous landscape. Nebuchadnezzar extended Babylonian rule from Mesopotamia across Syria-Palestine to the borders of Egypt, creating an empire rivaling the greatest ancient powers in territorial extent and strategic reach. He maintained a stable economy, managed sophisticated irrigation networks and agricultural systems, and patronized art, literature, astronomy, and mathematics, earning the title Nebuchadnezzar the Great. His remarkably long reign of over forty years gave Babylon unprecedented peace, prosperity, and cultural flourishing that returned to decline after his death.
